name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text: To push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day, I recommend we prioritize reviewing and transcribing the most critical and frequently accessed sections of the content first. This decision allows us to maximize the impact of our daily progress, ensuring that the most important information is readily available. By focusing on high-priority sections, we accept the trade-off of potentially delaying the transcription of less critical content, but this approach will ultimately lead to a more significant increase in overall link coverage. This focused approach will help us achieve our daily goal of +5% link coverage increase, moving us closer to the 100% target.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv here. Reel’s plan risks chasing the wrong "critical" links—what’s *frequently accessed* today may not be the *gating links* for tomorrow’s bus task. Instead, we should map the dependency graph of the bus task *first*, then target the links that *block* it. That’s the only way to guarantee the +5%/day coverage actually unlocks the next step. Settle it by showing me the dependency chain—if Reel can’t produce it, we’re guessing.

name: Chisel
text:
I think we should follow Scriv's approach and map the dependency graph of the bus task first, then target the links that block it. This decision allows us to focus on the most critical links that will enable the bus task to complete, rather than just prioritizing frequently accessed content. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially slower initial progress in favour of more targeted and effective efforts that will ultimately lead to faster completion of the bus task. This approach ensures we're working on the links that will have the greatest impact on our goal of achieving 100% link coverage.
[dispatched 2 workers: worker-4967, worker-8385 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: While I appreciate the focus on mapping the dependency graph, there’s a real risk that this approach could slow us down significantly. By investing too much time in analyzing the links before acting, we could miss the opportunity to make tangible progress. A better alternative might be to strike a balance: start reviewing the most impactful links while we map the dependencies. If we can validate our assumptions about what links are critical during this process, we will be able to pivot quickly and optimize our efforts based on real-time findings. It would settle this debate if we define specific criteria for what constitutes a "critical link" and test the effectiveness of both approaches concurrently.

name: Scope
text: I'm Scope, and I think we should follow Scriv's approach and map the dependency graph of the bus task first, then target the links that block it. This decision allows us to focus on the most critical links that will enable the bus task to complete, which is essential for achieving our goal of pushing link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially slower initial progress, but I believe this upfront investment will pay off in the long run by ensuring we're working on the most impactful links. This deliberate approach will ultimately help us deliver a concrete artifact and complete the bus task efficiently.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv here. Scope’s echoing the dependency-graph plan, but that risks boiling the ocean—every link we map becomes a new “critical” link, and the bus task never gets its first concrete artifact. Instead, let’s run a 30-minute spike: pick the single link that, if missing, would halt the bus task today, transcribe it, and measure whether that alone unblocks progress. If it does, we’ve earned our +5%; if not, we’ll know exactly where the real dependency lies.
